newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain regional debt offers high competitive yields.
newsitem.headline: Spain regional debt offers high competitive yields.

text.p: Investors hungry for high yield can find in Spain more than one way to satisfy their appetites.
Along with Spanish government bonds, they can buy regional issues, analysts said.

With total debt having sky-rocketed to 4.261 trillion pesetas ($33.45 billion) in June 1996 from 945 billion pesetas at the end of 1990, the 17 Spanish regional governments offer ample fare even for the heartiest appetites.

Up to now, Spain's steady shift toward fiscal federalism has been accompanied by a sharp rise in regional debt. But armed with a new right to collect taxes, analysts believe regional governments will become more virtuous in the future.

Spain's minority Popular Party government, which owes its parliamentary majority to allies from Catalonia and the Canary Islands, is set to approve a law that would enable regions to collect up to 30 percent of income tax revenue in two years.
"With the new system, we will likely see an improvement in the state of local finance," said Juan Jose Garcia, director at Standard & Poor's in Madrid.
From 1998, all regional governments will have the scope to change tax rates by up to six percent. They will also assume total responsibility for education and health expenses.
"The new system will be more transparent. Every single local government has to show how much they spend and how they fund it," Garcia said.
The transparency should add to the appeal of regional debt, analysts said.
"Regional debt is not 100 percent like central government bonds, but it is really close. And it offers higher yields," Manuel Navarro, dealer at Caja de Madrid told Reuters.
But not all regional debt is tradeable. Up to June 1996, a mere 34 percent was bonds, with the bulk made up of bank loans.

To increase the percentage of debt offered directly on the market, Catalonia, one of the most aggressive regions, inaugurated a new system of public auctions earlier this month. The new system should make issuances cheaper.
At its debut auction last week, Catalonia placed 10-year bonds at 15 basis points over their government equivalents.
Catalonia, rated A1 by Moody's and AA from Standard & Poor's, usually pays 20 to 25 basis points over 10-year government bonds.

Valencia, which began a similar public auction system to Catalonia's a few years ago, can fund its debt most cheaply for any region. Valencia,with a Aa3 rating from Moody's and a AA rating from Standard & Poor's, usually offers a spread of some 15 basis points over 10-year government bonds.
In total, Standard & Poor's has ratings on seven regions, ranging from Madrid with the lowest at AA minus to the Basque country at AA plus. The other five have been assigned an AA rating.
Moody's also rates the Basque Country Aa2, while Castilla y Leon, Andalucia have all been rate Aa3. Madrid stands at A1 and Murcia at A2.
To foreign investors, however, the secondary market can still be cheaper than public auctions because banks tend to bid up the price of the paper in the highly competitive auctions.
"Many times, these issues are cheaper on the secondary market," a dealer at Banco Central Hispano in Madrid said.
Financial institutions compete to offer good conditions to the regional governments in an effort to persuade the regions to bank with them, one dealer said.

In absolute terms, Catalonia has the highest level of debt, followed by Andalucia, Madrid and Valencia. In relative terms, Murcia has the greater level of debt with a 163.5 of debt over revenue (end 1994) followed buy Madrid at 147.5 (end 1995). ($1=127.4 Peseta)
